paragraphs.heading: Waves raised by wind
paragraphs.text: A wind wave is a surface wave that forms on the free surface of a body of water when wind blows over it. On Earth, the smallest wind waves are ripples and the largest are more than 30 m (100 ft) high. Wind is not the only thing that makes waves in water. Watercraft, animals, waterfalls, landslides and earthquakes can also generate them.

paragraphs.heading: What limits their size
paragraphs.text: Four things limit how big wind waves get: the speed of the wind, its duration, the fetch and the depth of the water. Fetch is the distance over which wind and water are in contact, measured along the wind’s direction. Duration is how long the wind has been blowing across the water. The wind must also outrun the wave crest for energy to pass to the wave. A fully developed sea has the largest waves theoretically possible for a wind of a given strength, duration and fetch. More exposure to that same wind could only cause energy to be lost, as wave tops break and form “whitecaps”.

paragraphs.heading: Ripples and sea waves
paragraphs.text: Ripples appear on smooth water when the wind blows, but they die quickly if the wind stops. The restoring force that lets them travel is surface tension. Sea waves form under sustained winds. They are motions on a larger scale and are often irregular. They usually last far longer, carrying on once the wind has died, and gravity is the restoring force that lets them travel.

paragraphs.heading: Swells that cross oceans
paragraphs.text: While a system of wind waves is being directly generated and affected by the local wind, it is called a wind sea. Once the waves move out of the area of fetch and the local wind no longer affects them, they are called swells, and they can travel thousands of kilometers. As waves move away from where they began, they naturally separate into groups that share a direction and a wavelength. One noteworthy case starts south of Tasmania, where heavy winds generate waves. They travel across the Pacific to southern California, where they produce desirable surfing conditions.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring a rough sea
paragraphs.text: In any one area the waves typically come in a range of heights. For weather reports and scientific analysis, their characteristic height is usually given as the significant wave height. To get it, take the highest third of the waves in a given time period and average their heights. It is also the value a trained observer, such as a member of a ship’s crew, would estimate by looking at the sea. On a particular day or in a particular storm, the biggest single waves will probably be a little under twice the reported significant wave height.

paragraphs.heading: Randomness and rogue waves
paragraphs.text: There is a certain amount of randomness in wind waves. Each wave differs from the one before in height, in duration and in shape, and predictability is limited. It is sometimes alleged that the seventh wave of a set is always the biggest. That is not the case, though the waves in the middle of a set do tend to be larger than the ones on either side. Individual “rogue waves” can also occur, standing much higher than the rest of the waves in the sea state. The Draupner wave was 25 m (82 ft) high, 2.2 times the significant wave height.
